utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by our intern, Jaspreet Saini, and Mr. Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as the Registrar, the legal officer, the usher, and the court reporter, and the interpreters who have been aiding us efficiently, as well as all the security officers. This is our 158th hearing, and we should conclude with the testimony of our witness, General Merdan. Defence counsel will now be putting questions to this witness that arise from the questions put to the witness by the Bench. Could the usher please call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General. I hope that all is well. As I said yesterday, this will be the last day of your testimony. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Bourgon who will be putting questions to you, I believe, unless his colleague will take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Madam Judge, good day, Your Honour, good day, Mr. President. We will first give the floor to our colleagues who represent the other accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll give the floor to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team have no additional questions that arise from the Judges' questions. Mr. Bourgon, I will give you the floor again. And you may place your lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have the opportunity of meeting at least twice before in Sarajevo. Nevertheless, for the benefit of the transcript, let me introduce myself this morning. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic. This morning, General, we will be conducting, as the Presiding Judge has mentioned, the last phase of your testimony in this case. Before I do so, I would like to come back briefly to something that was mentioned by the Trial Chamber yesterday with regard to memory. Now, I did not have too much to do last night, so I played the game of trying to remember where I was ten years ago. And I found it quite difficult. Now, of course, I was not the deputy commander of a corps which has more than 25.000 men. But nevertheless, I thought it was a very difficult exercise. So I just wish to take this opportunity to join the comments that were made by the Trial Chamber yesterday and to say how much everyone in the courtroom appreciates your effort over ten days in trying to remember all those details that we have been asking of you. Let me then proceed with a few questions. And I would like to begin, first of all, by coming back on an issue which was raised by -- on a number of occasions during your testimony. And General, I would like to know whether -- when you were reminded that you were testifying under oath before this Trial Chamber, whether you understood what that meant.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully understood what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after having spent almost ten days before this Trial Chamber, would that lead you to change any of the answers you have given to this day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't change any of the answers that I have given. I wouldn't change the substance of any of my answers. Perhaps I made a slip of the tongue at some point, but I informed the Chamber of everything I could remember. If I couldn't remember certain events, I mentioned this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. The first issue I would like to cover this morning is bringing you back to some of the questions which were asked of you by the Presiding Judge with respect to the weapons that were available to the 3rd Corps in 1993. Do you recall the essence of the questions which were requested of you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the essence of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask you a few additional questions with respect to weapons. Would you be able to enlighten the Trial Chamber with respect to the number of bullets that a soldier going into any combat task should be given according to the training that you have received.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Are you referring to the training I had in the former JNA or the training I obtained in the course of the war and after the war? One never stops learning; one never stops training. So perhaps you could put a more precise question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I will try to have a little more precise question. Based on your experience as a soldier, if soldiers under your command were to be assigned to a combat task, what would be the basic load that they would carry in terms of the number of bullets?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all armies throughout the world, there are certain established norms that are established when soldiers are assigned a task. These norms vary depending on the army concerned. I know that for a soldier in the former JNA, it was normal to have two combat sets and one reserve combat set. If the soldier were to go into action, to mount a defence or to engage in an attack, it depends on the type of action, the type of attack, for example. In certain conditions, the number of bullets is increased. As for the members of the 3rd Corps, I know that these norms, the norms of any army in the world, were not respected. I know that we couldn't even provide a soldier with half a combat set. If you have an automatic rifle, you need a lot of ammunition. We were not able to provide such ammunition. I remember that we would send soldiers to launch an attack with only 25 bullets for an automatic rifle. If you're aware of the number of bullets such a weapon can fire in one minute, then one might say that this amounted to nothing. We tried to tell our soldiers not to open bursts of fire, but save as much ammunition as they could. That was the situation in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you confirm some information which was provided by some witnesses before this Trial Chamber, that the actual Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond number of weapons which were available to a unit was in some cases one weapon for each three soldiers. Is that a ratio that is familiar to you based on your experience with the 3rd Corps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What makes the question a leading one, Mr. Mundis? You have objected. Defence counsel has asked the witness to mention the ratio he was aware of. I don't think that that would be a leading question, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was the first part of that question where my learned colleague put a statement to him, to the witness, and asked him to confirm a ratio that other witnesses have provided. And then in effect asked him either to agree or disagree with that. The way that entire statement and question were formulated suggests the answer to the question, in our respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Bourgon. Try to put the question in a neutral manner. I know that you are trying to be expeditious, but sometimes it is necessary to be cautious. Please proceed, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Naturally, this is an objection raised by my colleague that I anticipated. Mr. President, the witness has been testifying for ten days now, and on a number of occasions I refer to statements made either by the witness or by the Chamber or by the Prosecution. And the purpose of referring to these statements is to ask the witness to express his opinion. Although this may appear to be a leading question, since we're asking the witness's opinion, his answer is not going to be yes or no. The witness is only asked to say what he thinks about a certain matter. So I don't think it's a leading question, Mr. President. But I will do my best to put the questions in a neutral way. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would like to rephrase my last question and simply ask you, to your knowledge, what was the ratio of weapons per member within a unit of the 3rd Corps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ratio was fairly unfavourable. Not every soldier had a rifle. At the most critical locations, one soldier would have one rifle. At less critical locations, the ratio was worse. There would be one rifle for four soldiers. The weapons or the rifles they had were of very calibres and various types. There were ordinary rifles such as the ones used in the Second World War, and semi-automatic rifles that had been one of the more important weapons in the former JNA. There were automatic rifles of various calibres. None of this had been standardised. The men had no other weapons. If you observe a front line, you will notice that there are weapons that come from the First World War and weapons that are more contemporary. But we didn't have the most modern automatic rifles such as the ones used by NATO. So this was very outdated. Weapons had been used a lot as they weren't very precise. We didn't have time to clean the weapons. You probably know that it's necessary to clean the weapons regularly. The barrels have to be maintained. They have to be protected from rust. The conditions were very bad. There was fighting in the trenches, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like now to ask that the -- you be given the exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit 272, which will then be followed by exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit 192. Do you have this document, General?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Document 272 in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to ask you a -- some questions in relation to this document as a follow up to the questions that you were asked by the Presiding Judge. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to refer you inside this document to page 4. Do you see in the middle of page 4 that there is a breakdown of materiel and equipment in ten different tactical groups. The title of this paragraph is called "filling in the OE2 form," O for oscar, E for echo. Do you see this paragraph on page 4? The number of the page, to help you out, the -- what we call ERN number is 01821334, which appears in the top right corner of this document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like you to look at the list on this page, and then move on further down to page 8 of the document -- sorry, page 9. And page 9, the ERN number for this page will be 01821337.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found that page, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I see on this page, General, quite an impressive list of weapons, devices, and equipment. Did the 3rd Corps have this type of equipment in 1993? And I'd ask to take your time and look at sections 1, sections 2, and sections 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document be placed on the ELMO for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Have you had time, General, to go through the list under serial 1, which includes the way it is titled in English "weapons, devices, and equipment"; under serial 2, "ammunition, mines, and explosives"; and serial 3, "motor vehicles, trailers, carts, and other vehicles"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a brief look at these lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did this list, General, refer to equipment that you had in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is just a list which refers to the weapons in code, under codes. I don't think we had all these weapons, though. In 1993, people would also use or take some of their own weapons to the lines they were defending in a given zone. So the chief of staff recorded the numbers here so that it would be easier to follow and so that when reports were provided, the 3rd Corps can understand them more easily since the names used are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So am I to understand, General, that this is only a staff list, and that has nothing to do with the equipment that the 3rd Corps actually had in stock in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps did not have all this equipment at its disposal, at least not in the way it is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to give you a second document, which is Document Prosecution Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that the 3rd Corps did not have the weapons which are mentioned here? Is this the right understanding of your words? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've said that the 3rd Corps did not have all of the equipment and weapons that are on the list here. They did have some weapons and some equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it was a problem of interpretation. What you're saying is they did not have all of these weapons and equipment at their disposal, but just some. For example, RPG number 163, and it seems that there were 28 of those in one of the brigades, if -- I'm speaking from memory. Mr. Bourgon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I now refer you to Prosecution Exhibit 192. Do you have this document, General?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to this document, and to move to page 24. And this is a chart called "overview of the use of artillery ammunition."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this page numbered 01851616?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, General. Sorry, I should have mentioned that number.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am looking at that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you, General, look at these figures which represent the use of artillery ammunition and provide your opinion to the Trial Chamber as to whether the quantities in this chart allow you to conclude as to how much artillery ammunition the 3rd Corps had during 1993. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the standards of which I have already spoken earlier, what is shown here as the total figure for the entire corps is below the norm appropriate for a brigade. This was a minimum. At one point in time, I said that it would have been equal to 0 for a professional soldier. This number of artillery, bullets and shells, are not very conducive to an efficient combat. And I've said that this is below standard for a brigade, let alone for a corps which had over 10 brigades. If we talk percentages, this paints a very unfavourable picture for the corps which had between twenty-five and thirty thousand men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would just like to -- there was a document that I could show you now, but to gain time, a document highlighting the use of 3.000 rounds of artillery for a 24-hour operation by the HVO. Is that a possible figure in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved around quite a lot, and I had a lot of information. In addition to that, I heard shelling -- shells being fired by the HVO and the Serbian aggressor on our defence lines. I could hear the long-range artillery very well, and I could tell very well where the shells came from. You could tell exactly what direction the long-range artillery shots came from. Based on that, I could come up with somewhat more reliable estimates. I did not count the number and the frequency of shells, but I'm sure that there were a lot of shells being fired from the HVO and from the area under the aggressor, under the Republika Srpska Army. I'm sure that a lot of artillery ammunition was fired, both by the HVO as well as from the area under the control of the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can you in any way compare the artillery ammunition available to the 3rd Corps with that which was available to the HVO in 1993.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my rough estimates, the ratio was 1 to 10, 15, or even 20. If the army was able to fire one shell, then the HVO on their hand could have responded with 20 or even more shells. So I suppose this would have been an approximate estimate of the ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you -- in response to a question which you were asked concerning how you managed to obtain equipment throughout 1993, you mentioned that one of the sources was capture during operation. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how is it that capture during operations becomes a source of getting new weapons for you.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I said that capture of arms and equipment from the aggressor against Bosnia and Herzegovina and from the HVO was one of the sources of equipping and arming members of the 3rd Corps. When you look at the other possible sources, then this was the main source of supply of weapons and equipment for members of the 3rd Corps. I can say before this Trial Chamber that members of the 3rd Corps on a number of occasions captured arms and equipment. And I could give you individual examples on several occasions I witnessed when the 3rd Corps members captured weapons. On two occasions, I witnessed tanks being captured from the enemy. An army fighter came 80 metres close to a tank. He fired an anti-fire shell, and the tank was hit. It wasn't hit properly, but still, it had to stop. The aggressor soldiers fled from the tank, and our men brought a Caterpillar 8. This was a very heavy piece of engineering equipment in private ownership, and they towed the tank to a workshop where it was repaired. This tank was T84, and this is how we obtained we it. You can imagine how happy we were when we were able to get hold of two combat kits for this tank. It was a huge reward for us. I remember that event. We were celebrating all day when we managed to get hold of such a good tank and two combat sets for this tank. I could share with you a lot more details. I know that our men stormed into the trenches of the HVO and of the aggressor against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In those trenches, we would find thousands upon thousands of bullets and hundreds upon hundreds of shells. And this was the main source of supply for the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In response to questions that were put to you by the Trial Chamber, you had the chance to talk about the combat power of the HVO. How would you compare combat power of the HVO with that of the 3rd Corps, taking into account all factors that you said were relevant to this comparison; namely, weapons and human resources?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this Trial Chamber, I have already mentioned the factors that have an impact on the strength of a unit. Obviously, the number of troops and the number of weapons are the most important factors. In addition to that, the number of shells and the type of weapons are very important. If your weapons are outdated, if they're not modern, that puts you in a less favourable position. If you look and compare members of the HVO and members of the 3rd Corps, I can claim with certainty that the number of troops was in favour of the 3rd Corps. But the number of arms was in favour of the HVO. I had opportunities to see for myself when I was moving around as a member of joint commissions. I moved around the defence positions of the HVO as well as of the defence position of the BiH Army. I was with Mr. Franjo Nakic. I did not enjoy any privileges with regard to members of the HVO; however, I could clearly see that every member of the HVO was equipped with very modern automatic weapons. A member of the BiH Army, on the other hand, did not have a weapon each. If they had weapons, those were rifles of different calibres, of different makes. I've already said that we had rifles from the Second World War. There were semi-automatic rifles of the former JNA. There were very few automatic rifles. I even saw men on the line who had hunting rifles, unlike among the HVO who all had automatic rifles. I also know how many artillery pieces they had. I can also tell you that judging by the number of shells fired, the HVO had a huge advantage. As for the equipment that a soldier is supposed to carry, I had an opportunity to see the difference between the equipment of the HVO and the BiH Army soldiers. All the HVO soldiers had uniforms and shoes. Members of the 3rd Corps did not have uniforms. Some had only parts of uniforms. Some were in civilian clothes. Some wore tennis shoes instead of boots. I saw among the HVO that they had flak jackets which is a very important safety factor for an infantry soldier, for a foot soldier. And it also serves to increase such soldier's morale. On the other hand, members of the BiH Army, including the 3rd Corps, did not have any bulletproof clothes or vests. I could provide you with a lot more details to show you that there was a huge difference between members of the HVO and members of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, if I ask you for just a quick response. In terms of taking all those factors into account, which army was stronger, the more combat power: The HVO in terms of the central operative zone of CBOZ, or was it the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look at all this, you have to bear in mind that the main mission of the 3rd Corps of the BiH Army was to defend the state from the aggressor. And we never backed down from that mission. As members of the 3rd Corps, we had at least two-thirds of soldiers engaged in fighting with the Serbian aggressor, and those lines were never abandoned. The rest of the soldiers could have possibly been used and engaged against the HVO. Now, if you look at that ratio, and if you know that only one-third of our men could be engaged in fighting the HVO, and if you know that during the most fierce fighting in Central Bosnia, the HVO had abandoned all of their positions facing the aggressor, and they channelled all of their strength to engage in fighting at the BiH Army, and if you look at this complex problem, you may say that in this situation, the HVO was much more powerful and had a lot more advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And which army was stronger or had the strongest combat power between the Bosnian Serb Army and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian aggressor had a much higher combat power. When I was explaining things using the map, I told you that the 3rd Corps had to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond defend itself from an attack of one entire corps and two other Serbian aggressor corps which were not engaged only in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. In any military, when you're supposed to attack, you use a much stronger force than the army that defends itself. The aggressor had a huge advantage at the beginning of war. They had initial successes in taking territory. The aggressor's power was much higher than the power of the BiH Army, and the same situation could be felt in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. In other words, the aggressor was much more powerful than the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, if you put the HVO and the Bosnian Serb Army together facing the 3rd Corps, is there any way you can compare the combat power of these two entities?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already said something about that when I was talking about having just one front facing the aggressor. And then we had to open the second front facing the HVO. I've said here that the HVO and the aggressor against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina cooperated for a while. They were in agreement. During that period of time, the BiH Army had two enemies. On the one hand, we were facing the aggressor against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the other hand we were facing the HVO, which was an enemy during a period of time. So if I can come to a conclusion, I would say that we had the Serbian aggressor which was much more powerful than the units of the 3rd Corps, and on the other hand we had the HVO which in some of the elements had an advantage over the units which came in direct conflict with the HVO. You can imagine what was the situation that members of the 3rd Corps found themselves in. I believe that in the history of warfare, this had never been recorded or seen. I know that officers of foreign military forces who were aware of the situation, they admired our strength, and they really wondered how we could survive in such a situation with we were facing two much more powerful enemies. When I look back at that time today and when I compare what we were facing with the type of warfare today, I really don't know how we managed to survive and how we managed to defend ourselves from two enemies. I also answered questions with regard to the opening of the third front. Now, if the third front had been opened, can you imagine how difficult this would have been for us. And we would have certainly lost that war if that third front had been opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you simply explain to the Trial Chamber what kind of stress and obligation would such a situation impose on the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is very difficult to explain. You should be there in order to understand this. I believe that even my commander was not aware of how difficult the situation is and under what kind of stress he was. Sometimes when I talked to my friends, I tell them that it was absolutely beyond belief how he could cope with all that stress. When I was talking about losses, I told you that my commander is a very sensitive person. And if a soldier dies, one feels compassion. Can you imagine how he felt when thousands of people died? He was aware that he could not provide his men with enough ammunition, enough food, clothes. It is very difficult to put all this into words. You would have had to be there in order to understand. Only a person who had been through that can understand that. I've already told you that we had a very difficult situation when the aggressor captured Jajce, when we had a very difficult situation in the plateau of Vlasic. I was practically comatose at the time. I couldn't sleep for nights. I was hungry, but I couldn't eat. I didn't have any appetite. I know that my commander could not eat or sleep for days. I would find him in his chair day in, day out. During the night, he would sleep in the chair. He did not have the time to go to bed and have some rest. Those are moments which are very difficult to describe, explain, and put into words. To this very day, I don't stop wondering how he could survive all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You just mentioned something concerning the number of casualties. And this was a question put to you by the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber. And the figures mentioned were something like 1500 killed and 6400 injured. While you did not remember these figures, were you surprised by these figures?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the 3rd Corps had sustained casualties. This was the result of the balance of forces that I have just been talking about. There was no other way for us to defend our country. And this is why we sustained significant losses. If we had had good weapons, good equipment, the losses would certainly not have been so great. But such were the conditions we had to fight in. I think we managed to carry our mission out. We defended that part of the territory against the aggressor and against the HVO at the time. So if a professional soldier takes into account the number of victims and the mission that has to be carried out, well, then one might say that the victims served to accomplish their mission. I do know that each and every life is valuable, and the commanders try to do everything to prevent the loss of life. But commanders have to always bear in mind their main task; they have to bear in mind the manner in which they'll accomplish that task. So the losses were really grave. But nevertheless, the mission was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have one last question on this topic before moving on. And that is do you know if there was an ammunition factory in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and if so, where was it and who controlled it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A munition factory was in Konjic which was outside the 3rd Corps's zone of responsibility. But according to the information I had, there wasn't enough gunpowder in the factory to use for the weapons. We had quite a few connections. It was possible for us to produce shell cases, but we didn't have the explosives with which to fill those shells. So in the zone of the 3rd Corps, there were no factories that produced explosives. We couldn't produce shells for mass use. The amount that we could produce was very slight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, did the HVO have any means of producing explosives?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the main factory for producing explosives was in Vitez. It was under the control of the HVO. I have reliable information according to which that was the biggest factory of explosives in the Balkans, and it was one of the foremost factories in Europe and perhaps in the world. I know that the JNA would export explosives from Vitez to countries abroad. It was well known, this, in Europe and beyond. So the explosives factory was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, you are probably not an expert in explosives, but if I ask you that this factory in Vitez, blowing up such a factory, what would be the result?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the result would be a huge explosion with catastrophic consequences. I don't know what else I could say. That would be the briefest reply I could provide you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware, General, that there was a threat by the HVO to blow up the factory in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, we're aware that there were some questions put from the Bench on the weapons, but the Prosecution submits that we've gone way far beyond the scope of questions put by the Bench, and the -- these lines of questions are also irrelevant to the charges that the accused are here to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, in fact, we asked questions about ABiH weapons. You're asking about HVO weapons. And why not? But you are now dealing with the Vitez factory and the consequences of blowing it up. You see, you're going off on a tangent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll move on to another subject. But to ask whether a factory might be blown up, well, this might have an effect on the way in which command and control was exercised. That was the purpose of my question, but I'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, the second topic I would like to go over with you is Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond questions that were put to you by the Trial Chamber with respect to your own position in 1993 and when you had one or two positions. And my first question to develop on this issue is: Can you briefly explain what is a municipal defence staff.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A municipal defence staff is an organisation for defence within the structure of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's located in a given municipality. It's a Territorial Defence organisation for a given municipality. It was based on the structure of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And inside a municipal defence staff, what kind of units can we find and what is the average size of a municipal defence staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In municipal defence staffs, there were units that were called anti-sabotage detachments. This depended on the size of the municipality, but there would be two to three such detachments. In addition to the command of a municipal staff, the municipal staff also had smaller units for protection and smaller communication units. This was all linked to well-defined territory. Anti-sabotage detachments were organisations within the Territorial Defence, and they consisted of one to two companies. If it was one company, it was a stronger company, or it had two companies. Or a detachment had two companies and a platoon. So there were between 280 and 300 men in one such detachment. That was the way in which municipal staffs were organised. That's how they were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what is the difference between a municipal defence staff and a district defence staff.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A district or regional defence staff is the staff that is superior to the municipal staff. A district defence staff was responsible for a number of municipalities. A district defence staff had units of its own. They were not very large. I know that in terms of establishment, the Zenica district staff was to have a brigade, a protection company, a communications platoon. These are all fairly small units. And the brigade that the district defence staff was supposed to have consisted of about a thousand, a thousand and fifty men. So within the system of command and control, it's the command that is superior to the municipal defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And your position before being appointed as deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, can you specify between municipal defence staff and district defence staff? Which was it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was appointed as deputy commander in the 3rd Corps, I was commander of the district Territorial Defence staff for the Zenica area. This area included 13 municipalities. And my superior command was the Territorial Defence staff in Sarajevo, the Territorial Defence staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, as commander of the district defence staff, how many municipal defence staff reported to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 12 municipal staffs which were subordinated to the district Territorial Defence staff. They were subordinated since this all occurred within the system of command and control. That would be the more appropriate term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to ask the usher to provide the witness with Defence Exhibit 610, which is one of the new documents on the Defence list. We have copies here. I suggest maybe we can put it on the ELMO. Maybe you can show it to my colleague from the Prosecution before we do put it on the ELMO. Do you now have this document, General?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two documents. I don't know which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, the one that is presently on the ELMO, which is Defence Exhibit 610. Can you tell me where this document is from and who it is addressed to.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easier for me to look at the original, so I apologise if I read the document in this way. This document is from the supreme command staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief of the supreme command staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, reading this document, what is the purpose of the document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a proposal to resolve the status of district and municipal defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you turn, General, to this document, the last page looking at the person who has signed this document and tell us -- what can you tell us about the signature block of this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature block refers to the work group, to the deputy chief of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, do you know Jovan Divjak?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Jovan Divjak. He is a general in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina now, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, can you tell me whether on 29 January 1993 the status of district and municipal defence staff was an issue of interest to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The existence of a district staff was no longer a matter of interest for the 3rd Corps. That is why the district staffs were disbanded. But municipal staffs remained to cover certain territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would now like to refer you, General, to Defence Exhibit 629, which is a document dated on the 24th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you look at the document and explain exactly what this document is saying.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the supreme command staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The chief of the supreme command staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic, has signed this document. It's forwarded to the -- or it's addressed to all corps commands. And item one states that all municipal staffs should be maintained in their present function, especially as pertains to the districts and the running of local units based in the territory of the municipality. Item two says that municipal defence staffs should be maintained to unite the running of municipal staffs, cooperating, coordinating with the secretaries of defence, organs of the interior, and government organs in the territory, reduce the number of staff in the municipal staffs to 10 per cent of establishment. The corps commands will redeploy redundant personnel as they require.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like the usher to provide you with Prosecution Exhibit 320 as well as Prosecution Exhibit 245. And before those documents are given to you, General, can you recall when the district defence staff of Zenica was disbanded? Let's begin, General, with Prosecution Exhibit 320, a document dated 16th of April 1993. Can you read this document and inform the Trial Chamber whether you are familiar with the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the 3rd Corps command. It's an order to all municipal defence staffs. This document refers to district staffs and municipal defence staffs. The document says that the district defence staff in Zenica will be disbanded, and the command of the 3rd Corps, the organ for territorial structures will be taking over what was previously the responsibility of municipal defence staffs. Municipal staffs which aren't part of the district staff in Zenica have to carry out all the responsibilities they have with respect to the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to take you a look at Prosecution Exhibit 245, a document dated 18 November 1992 and inform the Trial Chamber whether you are familiar with the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the supreme command staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It has been signed by Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the chief of staff, the supreme command staff, Sefer Halilovic. This is an order for war duties in the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, could you look at where it says "order" under paragraph 1.A(ii), and inform the Trial Chamber as to what you see there.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A(i) says Enver Hadzihasanovic is appointed to position of corps commander. Number two says Dzemal Merdan is hereby appointed to the position of the deputy commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I now refer you to paragraph 2 of this order, and I would ask you to read this paragraph for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2: "The officers who have hereby been appointed as acting officers in accordance with this order will be relieved of their duties to date."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And what were your duties before being appointed as deputy commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was appointed as deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, as I have already said, I was the commander of the Zenica district staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, can you - if you know - inform the Trial Chamber whether a new commander was appointed to replace you as commander of the district defence staff.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. No one was appointed to replace me as commander of the Zenica district defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, during your testimony, you explained that when in a situation of war or other the commanding officer disappeared for some reason, that the chief of staff would take over until a new commander was appointed. Do you recall this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. I will try to be a bit more precise. Questions were put to you in respect to your position as commander of the district defence staff. Now, when you were relieved of your duties as commander of the district defence staff, what happened there if no new commander was appointed, as you say?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually an acting commander is appointed, especially since the district staff was also supposed to be disbanded. As I have said, this is an entire process. You can't just disband such a unit overnight. This requires a certain amount of time. So in such cases, an acting commander is appointed. Someone who isn't actually the commander, but someone who is just the acting commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this case, General, was an acting commander actually appointed for a district defence staff? And if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, the person who was appointed was Mr. Ramiz Dugalic. He was appointed the acting commander of the district defence staff of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you were asked a question by the Trial Chamber as to why -- during the period that you were relieved of your duties until the district defence staff was disbanded, why your name continued to appear on some documents of the district defence staff. In light of all answers you have just provided, can you explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district defence staff still existed. It was in the process of being disbanded. Now, when you look at the difference between disbanded and "in the process of being disbanded," there is the time that is required for such an institution to stop existing. There were still functions that the staff performed, and the 3rd Corps was still in the process of uniting all the defence staffs, and the 3rd Corps was still in the process of establishing a body within the 3rd Corps that would take over the duties. This is a transition period, a period that was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, one final question before the break: When the district defence staff was disbanded, what happened to Ramiz Dugalic who was then acting as commander of the district defence staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, when the position of the acting commander was abolished and when he stopped being in that position, he was appointed the head of the department for security within the 3rd Corps of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that it is the time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is 25 to 11.00. We will have a 25-minute break and we shall resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, we left off talking about the difference between district defence staff and municipal defence staff and your position. I would now like to address some questions which were put to you concerning the difference between offensive and defensive actions. Do you recall being asked questions in relation to such combat activities?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to provide the witness with Prosecution Document P799 as well as P800.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, I would begin with Document P799. And if you have this document, I would ask whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've never seen this document before. I recognise it as a document from the General Staff of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and this is the temporary regulations of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would like to you to turn to page 21 of this manual and to look at paragraph 65, which is the paragraph that was read to you by the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found page 21 in this document. However, I am not clear on the paragraph number. Did you say 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 65, sorry.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 65?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, page 21, paragraph 65. Have you found this page, General?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my copy, this is page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you read this paragraph, General, because I have a different page number.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read paragraph 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would ask you to read paragraph 65, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 65: "The commander bears full responsibility for the exercise of the task. He makes the decision, he issues orders to his subordinates, he organises coaction and cooperation and controls the exercise of the decision. He is responsible for the coordination of all the activities of his command, of his subordinate commands, and staffs as well as of the appropriate social and political organisations when it comes to the unification of combat operations and all the other forms of fight and general people's resistance in the zone of responsibility given to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In response to a question which was put to you by the Presiding Judge, you mentioned that you had not been commander of a corps and that applied specifically to a corps commander. However, I would like to ask you, because you have been working for three different corps commanders between 1993 and 1994, I would ask you to comment on this paragraph and explain, if you can, what is meant by "the commander bearing full responsibility for the accomplishment of a mission"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that, and I've read, that this rule existed in the former Yugoslav Army, and this was a temporary rule. As to bearing full responsibility in the former JNA was considered a very broad term. In the army, we believe that this responsibility was only for soldiers who were subordinate to this commander. This is the responsibility that we applied in our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, when we talk about the accomplishment of the mission, what is meant by "the responsibility for the mission"? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mission is something that is given in the form of a task to a subordinate unit. And as soon as that is done, it is this subordinate unit that is responsible for the task. However, when you look at the overall mission of the corps, the corps had its own basic mission. I've already spoken about that. The main mission of the corps command was to defend the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in its area of responsibility. And this is the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. This was the main mission, and the corps commander was responsible for this mission that he was given by his superior command. This was the main mission of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, of course, this manual was never in force in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I would ask you, based on your military experience, what should the corps commander focus on while he occupies the function of corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander focuses his entire attention to the accomplishment of his main mission. I said what the main mission of the corps commander was. This was the focus of his attention. This was his main task, his main duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will now ask you to turn to the second document which was provided to you, which is P800. And I would refer you to page 9 where it says "commander."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the page number. I didn't hear you too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry. The page number was page 14 -- sorry, page 9 in your version. And the ERN number is 00387498. And it says "commander."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, looking at the two first paragraphs, can you read this out loud for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Corps commander: Commands over all the corps units and all the units attached to it in the zone directly or indirectly through the chief of staff, through his deputy, and through chiefs of branches. "He commands the corps command directly. He issues tasks to his subordinates. He controls the accomplishment of these tasks and bears full responsibility for the accomplishment of these tasks and for the overall situation in the corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Am I to understand, General, from this paragraph that if the mission fails, the commander is responsible; and if the mission succeeds, the commander is responsible?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, do you see a difference between military responsibility as we find it in this paragraph and legal or criminal responsibility of a person?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, I will try to make my question more precise. In this paragraph, we speak of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I authorise you to put this question. The Judges have not put this question to the witness. However, I still will allow you to put this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that this question stems from the Judges' questions, and I thank you for your permission to put it to the witness anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, the -- in this paragraph that we just read, we speak about the responsibility of a commander for the corps and for the mission. Now, in your -- to your knowledge, and that is, of course, if you know, do you make a distinction between the responsibility of a commander to accomplish his mission and the responsibility of a commander for crimes that he may commit?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander is responsible for the accomplishment of his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will move on now to -- if you go a little up on this page where we have "the duties of a corps command." And I would ask you simply to look at these issues, including what the duties of a corps command are, and confirm whether you would agree that these are, indeed, the duties of a corps command. Sorry, General, I will maybe -- I was just referring you to page 9, paragraph 2, and asking you to confirm whether the duties of a corps command relate to the list that is on that page.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go over all of the duties of the corps command and its bodies. There are a number of pages here. But only this would allow me to answer your question completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this case, General, I would simply ask you to focus on the duties of the commander personally which you find starts at the bottom of page 9 and continues at the top of page 10. And I would ask you to read all of the duties of the commander and to inform the Trial Chamber whether all of these duties are indeed what a commander does.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have gone through the main duties of a commander as they are listed in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on your experience, General, working with at least three different corps commanders, is that what can be expected from a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in response to a question which was put to you by the Trial Chamber, you mentioned the words "operational" and "strategic." The Prosecution expert witness explained that there were three levels of command and control, which were tactical, operational, and strategic. Can you provide the Trial Chamber with your opinion as to whether these three levels also applied to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The same expert witness for the Prosecution said that a commander at the operational level needed to focus a minimum of four days ahead. Would you agree with the expert for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the situation. I've testified before this Trial Chamber that the corps commander has to think ahead. And this is the essence of his operative thinking. Sometimes it can be four days or five days ahead. This depends on the situation. In any case, I claim that any commander at that level has to think ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you define for the Trial Chamber in order that we try to clarify the issue of military operations as you understand military operations to be.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "military operations" in my view implies the totality of combat operations and actions of operational and strategic significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm for the Trial Chamber whether the corps -- at which level do we find the corps when we speak of tactical, operational, and strategic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps is at the operational level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So are we to understand, General, that military operations, to your understanding, would be operations conducted by a corps using all of its assets at once?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Operations may be carried out by one corps or by two corps. If it is just one corps that is involved in operations, then yes, only for one corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, did the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina conduct any military operations in your understanding of the term in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, the 3rd Corps was engaged in Defence operations. It was never engaged in any assault operations. It was engaged only in Defence operations because this was its operational mission. The mission was to defend the territory that had come under the attack of the aggressor against Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was the operational mission of the 3rd Corps, defence. The 3rd Corps was never engaged in any assault operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, did any units of the 3rd Corps conduct combat activities at the tactical level during 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One may say that in certain periods of time, lower tactical units were engaged in tactical combat actions. But those were not operations. There's a difference between an action and an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at the tactical combat activities, this was a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, are there such things as defensive tactical combat activities and offensive tactical combat activities?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're considering the entire year of 1993, then in the 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility, there are both offensive tactical activities and defensive tactical activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At page 13.597 of the transcript, an example was given of a tactical offensive operation. In order for the Trial Chamber to understand the differences between the types of operation at the tactical level, I would simply ask you to qualify different examples, the first one being for a company to occupy an elevation where there is no enemy presently. How would you qualify such activity?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a company is attacking an elevation defended by the enemy which was always present at that elevation, then this is an offensive tactical action. If at that elevation, before the enemy took that elevation, that unit or that company or part of that unit was present there, well, in such a case, this is an offensive defence because you have to take up the position at that elevation. That is how I used to interpret this, and that is how I interpret it now, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, if a company occupies an elevation and holds this elevation in order to prevent the enemy from capturing this elevation, how would you describe such combat activity?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question. Was the enemy present at that elevation or not? This is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will say again this question. A company occupies an elevation where there is no enemy but stays on the elevation to prevent an enemy from taking the elevation.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't consider that to be combat action. All that is is taking up defensive position. This doesn't involve combat action, unless an enemy sabotage group infiltrates the area. But if there is no combat, we can't talk about combat action. This is a matter of taking up tactical position, and it doesn't involve any combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And last scenario, General: If a company occupying an elevation loses the elevation and then succeeds in taking it back a few hours later, how do you describe such combat activity?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that that is practically speaking an offensive defence because this elevation might be lost for various reasons, and the elevation might be very important for the company. Combat ensues, and the company takes the elevation again. This is an offensive defence. The unit engages in combat to regain the elevation it previously had. If they continued with their attack from that elevation, then we could talk about an offence, an actual offence, an actual attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, in both defensive and offensive combat activity, is it possible, and even likely, that weapons will be fired?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fire would be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when we look at the corps commander, you've told us that he was at the operational level. Is it -- are we to understand that the corps commander does not focus on tactical combat activities unless they are of an operational importance?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander is involved in tactical combat activities if such activities are in the vicinity of some operative feature or if those -- or if that tactical combat might threaten some sort of tactical target.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you were asked many questions about the combat activities which took place in the Dusina area. And my question would be: In your opinion, would the Lasva Valley junction qualify as an operational feature?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already explained, it's very important to have good communications for a unit. The Lasva junction is the most important road in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. It's important to have good roads, functional roads. And that is why this feature had operational importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to move on to the -- what actually happened in Dusina. I don't want, of course, to ask over again everything that was asked of you already. I would just like to go back in time a bit so that we understand what gave rise to the events in Dusina. And my first question would be: The combat activities which took place in Dusina, was that an isolated incident, or was that part of a series of events which started before that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified about this subject. I'll just try to be more precise now. It's necessary to bear in mind the exact dates and gain a view of what took place at a given date and to see what the causes were. I said that there was combat in the area of Busovaca on the 25th of January 1993. HVO units were very successful along the axis in the direction of the Lasva junction from Kaonik via the village of Katici and then Medeni towards Lasva. It was necessary to take up positions there in order to stop the HVO advance in the direction of the Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, the -- you mentioned Busovaca. Was Busovaca the origin of the events in Dusina, or can we go even further back to find the origin of those events?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it was quite clear to me that the HVO wanted to take control of the wider area around the Lasva junction in order to gain control of a very important road, a road that had operational significance for the 3rd Corps. Naturally, when I now look back to those events, the HVO was very successful on the 25th of January. Their objective was to take control of the area around the Lasva junction. And this feature was of exceptional importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, in many documents which were shown to you in respect of those events, there was mention of fighting in Gornji Vakuf. In your opinion, was the fighting in Gornji Vakuf related to the fighting in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was combat that took place in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. This was important for the corps command because this is something that took place in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, given that you were involved in those activities, can you recall when the fighting in Gornji Vakuf took place and what the HVO was attempting to do at that time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was in the area of Gornji Vakuf. That was in mid-January 1993. And the HVO wanted to take Gornji Vakuf. The fighting was fierce, the fighting to take control of the entire area of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did the 3rd Corps expect such activity in Gornji Vakuf, or were you taken by surprise?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that they expected such an action in Gornji Vakuf. We were taken by surprise up there because at the time, we believed that the HVO shared our objective, which was to defend ourselves from the aggressor. We didn't expect to be attacked by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this point, I would like to produce three new documents. I would like to show the witness three new documents which have to do with events in this area. And we have copies for the witness, the Chamber, and for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll wait until we see the new documents. But of course, if it goes beyond the scope of questions put by Your Honours, we would respectfully request the right to put some additional questions to the witness concerning the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I have understood you correctly, you wanted to explain the events in Dusina in relation to what took place in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our objective is to show the cause of the events in Dusina and to show why the commander acted in a certain way. But this won't take very long, and we will only be using these several documents to demonstrate the link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are three documents or five documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are five documents, but two are on our list and three were not on our list. The two documents on our list are DH554 and DH562.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where are the three new documents from?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these documents come from -- just a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will help us to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first two documents are dated the 12th and the 13th of January. And they come from the Sarajevo collection, whereas the third document comes from the Defence's archives, but it is directly linked to the two other documents as the Chamber will be able to note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these three new documents on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Principally, you should ask for leave. We are granting you leave to use these three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, may I ask you to look at those three documents very quickly. The first document is dated 12 January, and the ERN number is 01822083. The second document is dated 13 January 1993, and the ERN number is 01822089.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have that one. The document dated the 13th of January, we don't have that one. Apparently, we have been given two copies of the same document, the document dated the 12th. So that's the document dated the 13th January.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are three documents. Two are dated the 12th of January, and one is dated the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so there are two documents that are dated the 12th of January. There are two documents dated the 12th of January. The numbers is 119 and 120. These are the 3rd Corps numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third document, which is dated the 13th of January, has the 3rd Corps number 128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 128, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There are three documents, the first two dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Mundis, can you find your bearings? There's a document dated the 12th of January from the 3rd Corps signed by General Hadzihasanovic which was forwarded to the 314th and 7th Brigade. On the same date, the addressee is the same, but the number is 120. That's the number -- the first one was 119. The first paragraph is identical to the previous one; it's the second paragraph that changes. The third document, number 128, was forwarded to the district staff and the municipal staff, and it's dated the 13th of January. What would you say about this, Mr. Mundis? Are there any objections that you have to these documents that come from the 3rd Corps and relate to the 7th Brigade and have been signed by the 3rd Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I now have the three documents. Our objection is not so much to the documents at this point; it's to this line of questioning which in our respectful view does not arise from questions put by Your Honours concerning Dusina, and certainly could have been covered in the direct examination concerning Dusina had the Defence opted to do so. And our view is questions coming from Your Honours should be directly and closely linked to that, and it's not an open invitation to conduct direct examination anew with new documents with issues that could have and should have been put to the witness during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, would you like to respond. But we have granted you leave to use these documents. So it would be best to proceed since in the documents relating to Dusina, there was an entire series of orders signed by the 3rd Corps commander. And reference was made to an exacerbation of tension between the ABiH and the HVO. And in Document 119 and Document 120, we can see that there is a reference to the relation between the HVO and the ABiH. It all seems to be quite coherent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would simply ask you to look at these three documents, and considering that you were involved in these events, whether you can conclude or offer your opinion as to how the 3rd Corps reacted to the events forced upon it by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the 3rd Corps could do at that time was to raise the level of combat readiness of the forces that weren't engaged against the aggressor. So units or parts of units which were on leave or which were absent, in such cases, the 3rd Corps could order that these units attain a state of readiness because when there was combat in Gornji Vakuf no one knew how things would develop. So this is what the 3rd Corps had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will now move on to the next document, which is Defence Exhibit 554, also dated 12 January and bearing number 02/31-94. General, I would ask you to read the document. And if you can explain to the Trial Chamber what the purpose of this document is and what the corps commander is doing at that time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to mention the number it was registered under in the corps, to make sure that I'm reading the right document. The document is 02/31-94 dated the 12th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, General.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic sent to the supreme command staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
