It states the following: "Subject, our document, 02/31-91 dated the 11th of January 1993. It is clear that you have informed the Presidency. Tell us what to do at this moment, whether to accept a conflict or not, and how to resolve the problems that have emerged, taking into account your order to avoid a conflict at all costs."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain this document or what the corps commander is doing by this document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way I interpret this document. The commander faced major problems in Gornji Vakuf. Obviously, he couldn't decide whether to accept a conflict or not. He asks his superior command how to deal with the problems, taking into account the fact that he had a standing order to avoid a conflict with the HVO at all costs. The corps commander was faced with a dilemma. BiH Army units were being attacked up there, and the commander had to avoid a conflict at all costs. The commander was facing a dilemma. He asked for advice and position of his superior command. He wanted to hear from them whether to engage in a conflict or not because the commander was not in the position to deal with the problem himself, bearing in mind that he had his orders to avoid a conflict with the HVO at all costs. That was the dilemma that the corps commander was facing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your opinion, General, even though you have not been a corps commander, is this good commandership at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the commander's decision was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'll now refer you to the next document, Defence Exhibit 562 dated 13 January 1993 bearing number 02/33-130. Do you have this document, General?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have three specific questions, the first one being: In the first two sentences, the commander is saying "to firmly hold the line, reach towards the Chetniks, and to use those forces ready against attacks by the HVO." Can you explain what is meant by the commander in those two sentences.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said what this meant. "Hereby the commander issues orders to the troops not to abandon their lines facing the Chetniks, i.e., the aggressor against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and that the rest of the forces which were not engaged against the Chetniks should be put on the ready, on the highest level of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, the last paragraph on this document where it begins which "I assure you that holding back..." Can you read this paragraph for yourself and explain the meaning of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this paragraph. And the way I interpret it is as follows: Holding back from an open conflict with the HVO was yet another victory equal to any victory in a battlefield. "Should a conflict be unavoidable, you will be informed in time," which means you will be informed if I am forced to engage in combat against the HVO. I've read in the previous document that the commander was faced with a dilemma, and he wanted to hear what the position of his superior command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Based on these observations and these documents, in your opinion, was it normal in this context for the corps commander to be directly involved in the coordination of these activities in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very obvious that the commander is very interested in the situation in Gornji Vakuf. And the commander is faced with a dilemma that he can't resolve himself. However, he does whatever is in his power. He issues orders for his troops to continue holding the lines facing the Chetniks, i.e., the aggressor against Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that these lines should not be abandoned. As for the rest of the troops of the 3rd Corps, they should be put on the ready because if a conflict with the HVO cannot be avoided, then these troops will have to be engaged. However, this engagement should be preceded by a consent of his superior command. That is why the commander consults his superior command because he has his previous orders according to which he should avoid a conflict with the HVO at all costs. This is a huge dilemma which burdens the commander quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, given that you were involved in these activities, did this result in combat activities and armed conflict between the HVO and the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was up there. My mission was to try and resolve the problem in a peaceful way. I did my utmost with the mediation of the English UNPROFOR, the company of which was in Gornji Vakuf, to resolve the problem. However, combat activities continued in the area of Gornji Vakuf. These combat activities ranged in scale, and this is what the situation was in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, moving on closer to the combat activities which took place later in January in Dusina, you've had the opportunity during your testimony to describe how General Hadzihasanovic deployed his troops. My only question at this time is: Was it normal for him to deploy troops to such a low level as he did, giving orders even for the deployment of companies?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained why sometimes a tactical level may be of significance for the operation level. In this particular case, the feature in question was the Lasva junction. It was normal for the commander to deploy troops to defend the Lasva junction in the general area of that junction. The Lasva junction could not be defended only on the junction itself, and the troops were aware of that. Certain elevations had to be taken in order to prevent anybody from accessing the Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, do you recall the Presiding Judge asking you a question concerning Elevation 852. Now, that was on Document P128, which I can give you if need be. But do you recall those questions being asked?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the Chamber has put a question to me quoting the elevation. I believe that it was a general question asking me to explain the general conditions of attacking an elevation or a trig point. And that's how I answered. Obviously, it's very important if you know which elevation it is. I was not shown any specific elevation. And the way I understood the Trial Chamber's question was that they want me to explain the difference between assault and defence. And I did make a difference there. Maybe I have misunderstood the questions put to me because of the errors in interpretation that I received in my mother tongue. I believed that it was a general question involving combat operations around any elevation. I didn't hear the Trial Chamber giving a specific number, the specific number of a specific elevation point. I believe that it was a general question that could be applied to any elevation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would just ask you to take a quick look at Document P128. And from the reading of this document, can you confirm whether this was meant to be an offensive combat activity, or in other words was this meant to be an attack when the order refers to Elevation 852.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I understand this order, this is an order for defence. This is not an order for an assault in relation to the Elevation 852. I am familiar with the area, and now that I have looked at the specific elevation point and the line that is given leading up to this elevation point, I can say that at that time there were no HVO units on that elevation point. This elevation point was of the utmost importance for the defence of the Lasva junction. This elevation point was taken without any attack actions. This elevation point was free. There were no enemy soldiers there. This was not an assault action. This was a defence action, and it says here that this was an action to take positions for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to ask you a few quick questions as a follow up to the Trial Chamber asking you whether the 3rd Corps command requested reports from the field and actually received information from the field. So my first question would be: Can you tell me what was the standard practice within the 3rd Corps with respect to the submission of reports.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this Trial Chamber, I've already testified about the practice that was in place. Subordinate units were supposed to send their reports to their superior command. In this case, those were the subordinate units of the 3rd Corps which sent their reports to the 3rd Corps command. Those reports could be periodical, could be regular, it could be daily, weekly reports which all depended on the preceding orders. In any case, they should have been daily reports. In addition to that, there were also interim reports which were sent whenever something extraordinary was taking place in that particular unit. It was customary for the 3rd Corps command to receive both regular and interim reports from its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I use a concrete example to illustrate what you've just said: If a company which belongs to a specific battalion which, of course, belongs to a brigade, was resubordinated to a different brigade, my question is would it be normal for this company to submit two reports? One, to the unit to which it has been resubordinated; and a second one to the battalion to which it belongs with the aim of keeping its chain of command informed of its activities?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I have to point out a very important fact here. Our officers were not trained. They had not completed military education. We had major problems with reporting. You have to be aware of the situation that we were facing. When the line of command is in place, where everything is organised, where there are good means of communications, it is a customary practice for a resubordinated unit to send its report to the command that it has been resubordinated to, rather than to its usual command. However, that unit can report to its original command, the command from which it was resubordinated to another command. We had cases in practice that due to the lack of education among other officers, such reports would end up in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, could this explain that two reports would end up at the corps for the activities of the same detachment or company?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the specific documents. I said that this was possible. I'm not excluding that possibility, and I've just explained to you why this could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The practice of requesting reports from units deployed in the field and of obtaining information at regular intervals, can you provide your opinion as to whether this is helpful in terms of command and control?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this is very helpful. It is very helpful to have as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, going back to the events in Dusina, do you recall being shown a number of reports in this courtroom which were submitted by the units involved in the combat activities which gave rise to the allegations of murder by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this courtroom before this Trial Chamber, I have been shown some of those reports. I've had an opportunity to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is an error in the transcript. Maybe it is me who has expressed myself. It is the HVO that made allegations that crimes were committed. It is page 52, line 4. So there were no activities which gave rise to the allegations of murder by the HVO; it was rather the HVO that alleged that murders had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned that the events in Busovaca were directly related to what took place in Dusina. Can you provide further information as to what was happening in Busovaca at the time and what the HVO was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO tried to disarm members of the BiH Army and to take over control in the entire area of Busovaca. I've already said that the combat operations in Busovaca was -- were launched on the 25th of January 1993. The goal was for the HVO to take over control and power in the entire territory of the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you were asked some questions about the meeting on the 26th of January. In your opinion, what was the aim of that meeting that you attended on 26th January?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal was to stop combat in Busovaca and to resolve the situation in Busovaca in a peaceful way, to put an end to the combat operations in Busovaca. That was the goal of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you were asked also a number of questions about the visit to the site in Dusina. And my interest is not so much as to exactly what happened during the visit, but what was not asked so far is what was the aim of going to Dusina?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal of our visit to Dusina was for us to see what the situation was, whether everything was destroyed there as the representative of the HVO had alleged. They said that a crime had been committed there. Representatives of the HVO wanted to see for themselves what the situation was there. They did not have any other possibility to visit this area. That's why they used this joint commission in Busovaca. I've already said who its members were. It was an opportunity for the HVO to see for themselves what had taken place in the territory of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions in respect of what you concluded from all the reports that you saw. Now, my question at this point is the result of this visit to Dusina, did it confirm your views with respect to the reports that you had read?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My positions were confirmed. Mr. Franjo Nakic who was the representative of the HVO could see it for himself. Dusina and its broader area were not damaged. No houses had been set on fire. We could see that there had been fighting going on there, but it was on a low scale. From our conversations with the locals and from what the local commander told us at the moment, we could conclude that there had been combat there. But we also realised that no crimes had been committed there, or at least none of the persons that we spoke to told us anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, can you confirm that your knowledge of the investigation taking place and the involvement of the municipal defence staff in this matter also confirm your views that you concluded from reading those reports?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that confirmed what I had learned from the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as a final question in this area, at the time, General, based on all the information that you had, did you have any reason to believe that the HVO allegations might be true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the body of the knowledge that I acquired from the reports that I read and my visit to the site that was organised a few days later, and all the other information that I had had an opportunity to gather, I am convinced that no crime was committed there. There was combat there. There were casualties on both sides during combat. On the side of the HVO as well as on the side of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm whether General Hadzihasanovic held the same views as you did?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm convinced of that. General Hadzihasanovic was of the same conviction. He was of the opinion that there had been combat over there. I'm absolutely sure that this was what he firmly believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that we have reached the time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to remind the Defence, they have 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll try to be as fast as possible and make my questions as short as possible, and I will ask the General to make his answers as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We will resume at 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, we have 45 minutes. Don't despair. It's almost over. I'd like to ask you a few questions now with respect to the events in Miletici. You were shown by the Trial Chamber Exhibit P148 which provides some details about the perpetrators, including something about triangle police badges, and the name of one as being Ramadan. Can you confirm that you were -- what you were told by these villagers and whether you had any of this information at the time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and this is what I have said before this Chamber, I was told by the inhabitants that the crimes in Miletici were committed by men whom they called the mujahedin. At the time, I don't remember them mentioning someone by the name of Ramadan, nor do I remember them mentioning them having badges in the form of triangles on the clothes they were wearing. I did not hear such information from the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: While you were in Miletici, did you encounter any soldiers from the 3rd Corps; and if so, did you do anything in this respect?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone in the village of Miletici, apart from UNPROFOR representatives and the delegation that was present in the village of Miletici. There were no inhabitants there, and there were no troops as far as I could see when I observed the village of Miletici and when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And while travelling to Miletici, do you recall at some point in your testimony you mentioned meeting with members of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can remember, I never said that on my way to Miletici I met members of the corps. On my way to Miletici, I was in an armoured personnel carriers that belonged to the British Battalion. We did not stop on our way to the village of Miletici, and I did not see any 3rd Corps members while I was travelling to the village of Miletici. And this has been my testimony before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What measures, if any, did the 3rd Corps take with respect to the village in Miletici after what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but as far as I can remember, some measures were taken. The command of the 306th Brigade was ordered to look into the event. I have testified about this before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you mentioned your conclusions that from what the villagers told you, and you also mentioned and replied to some questions that Franjo Nakic had also spoken to the villagers. Do you recall if Franjo Nakic -- what Franjo Nakic told you, if anything, in terms of what he considered the event to have been?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this is translated, but I think that there are translation errors again. I believe that Franjo Nakic moved people to Miletici, but I'm claiming that Franjo Nakic -- I did not meet any people in the village of Miletici. As far as I can remember, it was when we were returning from the village of Miletici that we met inhabitants who said that they were from Miletici. This is a huge difference. We met these people outside of the village. I don't know how this is being interpreted into English, but I would not want to confuse you. When Franjo Nakic and I spoke to inhabitants from the village of Miletici, this was not in the village of Miletici. It was outside of the village of Miletici. It was when we were returning from the village of Miletici. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, General. I'm sorry, I was asking the wrong, with not enough details, my questions. What I'm interested in is whether Franjo Nakic drew the same conclusions you did following your encounter with the villagers, and if you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know about that. That's what Franjo Nakic told me. His conclusions were the same as mine, at least that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall what the Busovaca joint commission of which you were a member did after leaving Miletici that day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be clear. I don't want to mix anything up. At that time, the mixed commission worked in Vitez. It no longer went to Busovaca. There were local commissions in Busovaca, but the commission of which I was a member on behalf of the army, it had its headquarters in Vitez. It was no longer in Busovaca. It was near the English battalion. There was a private house which is where we were located, and that is where the joint commission was. Please, put a precise question to me. It was the joint commission after the events in Miletici and Vitez. Is that the joint commission you're referring to? Are you referring to a local commission which is still in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once again, General, I'm sorry. I'm trying to go quick, and I'm not providing you with sufficient information. I was simply thinking the commission that day, did you visit any other places, or did the visit to Miletici result in the work for the day being finished?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the visit to Miletici, we finished our working day in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next day, did you work with the commission; and if so, was Mr. Nakic there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we worked on the following day. And Mr. Nakic was there, together with me, at the same time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, if you recall, did Mr. Nakic come back on the events in Miletici that day with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but we did speak to each other. And Franjo Nakic expressed the same opinion that I had. I can't remember all the details, but I have mentioned the substance of that discussion. As to whether Franjo Nakic spoke to me about any other subjects, I can't remember now. I wouldn't exclude the possibility. If Franjo Nakic says that we had a discussion, well, that's something I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next day, when the work of the commission resumed, did Franjo Nakic complain to you about the events in Miletici, or did you move on to other incidents?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we had finished discussing the events in Miletici, and we had started addressing the issue of other incidents that had taken place in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, the Trial Chamber, when asking you questions about the events in Miletici, referred to a -- some type of investigation having been conducted by the Centre for Human Rights. And my question to you is did you ever meet these people or were you ever visited by anyone asking you questions about these events?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really can't remember anyone coming to discuss the events in Miletici. I have already said before this Trial Chamber that I had numerous meetings with representatives of international organisations, and I really don't remember members of a certain organisation coming to ask about the events in Miletici. I don't remember having discussed this particular subject with any such representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, can you tell me, after all these years, whether at the time you had any reason to doubt concerning your conclusion that the perpetrators in Miletici were mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of everything that I have been shown, and believe me, at the time I was also convinced that the mujahedin had committed the crimes in Miletici given what the inhabitants had informed me of, there are no two ways about this. I have no doubts about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, you have already in response to a question from the Trial Chamber confirmed that you had given that information and discussed those events with General Hadzihasanovic. If you can, can you tell us if General Hadzihasanovic shared the same views as you held with respect to the perpetrators of these events in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that General Hadzihasanovic shared my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, one last question on Miletici: Today, 11 years later, or even more, do you have any doubts as to the fact that the perpetrators in Miletici were, in fact, mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, even today, I have no doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move on now to the issue of mujahedin which was discussed with you by the Trial Chamber in the form of many questions. And the first thing I'd like to ask you is you mentioned as part of the context of the meeting which took place in April, if I recall correctly, you mentioned four events that were significant in April, including the kidnapping of Zivko Totic, the information provided to you in this respect by the ECMM some days later, to the fact that this -- that the Totic kidnapping had been done by mujahedin, your meeting with Sefer Halilovic, and the events in Miletici. Is that, in a nutshell, the four events that you referred to in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the situation in Central Bosnia at the end of April, can you describe what was the priority of the 3rd Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1993, the 3rd Corps' priority was to defend the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps against the Serbian aggressor. This was at all times its main task. That was our main task. In addition to what I have mentioned, the 3rd Corps continued to train its members. In April, there was fierce fighting with the HVO. In Vitez Municipality, the fighting was really fierce. There was large-scale combat and small-scale combat in the area of Gornji Vakuf and in the area of Busovaca, in Novi Travnik. The 3rd Corps focussed on these tasks, too, but the main task was to defend the territory against the aggressor in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, when you mentioned the fighting in Vitez Municipality, fighting that was really fierce, was there a reason for this fighting in the Vitez Municipality, or what caused the eruption of the fighting in the Vitez Municipality in April?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-April 1993, there are two exceptionally large-scale combats in Vitez Municipality. This was the attack of the HVO on Ahmici. And the wider area of the village of Ahmici. Then there was also intense fighting in the centre of the town of Vitez, the direction of the locations, the part that we called Old Vitez, Stari Vitez. And in other villages in Vitez Municipality, there was large-scale combat. In Gacice, Veceriska, Gornji and Donja Kruscica, and in many other villages there was such combat. These are villages in the Municipality of Vitez where there was combat in the month of April. But on the whole in April, as far as the relations between the HVO and the ABiH are concerned, the most intense fighting was in Vitez Municipality in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as a result of Ahmici, General, do you recall trying to establish a cease-fire between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO towards the end of April with the help of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very important task of the joint commission, and I've already said that in April its headquarters was in Vitez. So the main objective of that joint commission which was under the auspices of the European Monitoring Mission. The main task was to stop combat activities in Vitez, to stop them from spreading. As a joint commission, we could not accomplish this task. We could not stop combat activities in Vitez. There were a number of attempts, and I know that the international community endeavoured to help. We in the joint commission tried very hard. However, the developments were such that we could not stop the conflict in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall the difficulties in convincing members of the 3rd Corps to accept the cease-fire and the actions taken by both commanders in-chief at the time for this purpose? And I'm talking about, of course, Petkovic and Halilovic. Do you remember what they did during that period?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cease-fire agreement was signed, and all the troops were instructed to withdraw from the lines and to fill in the trenches on both sides. I remember that. This was in April 1993. An order to that effect came from Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was there a relationship between the actions taken by Mr. Halilovic and his presence in the Vitez Municipality at the time? Is that why he was there, or were there any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the main task was to reach an agreement on cease-fire between the HVO and the BiH Army in the Lasva Valley. And that's why the meeting was held in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to refer now to the meeting which was discussed with one of the Judges of the Trial Chamber during which General Hadzihasanovic decided to inform the supreme command of the problems or of the situation with respect to the mujahedin. In your opinion, General, is it possible that General Hadzihasanovic had the opportunity before this meeting to inform General Halilovic of the situation?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether there were any discussions between my commander, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, and Sefer Halilovic about that. I know that the communications were very bad, that we practically did not have any communication with the superior command in Sarajevo. I really do not have this information, or I can't remember. I cannot say with any degree of certainty whether this is true or not, because I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, immediately preceding the meeting, is it -- would it have been normal for your commander, General Hadzihasanovic, to have a tete-a-tete with General Halilovic before the official meeting which took place late at night? Were you aware of such a meeting or of the possibility of such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be a normal procedure. I believe that they did have an opportunity to get together before the meeting started. It would be normal procedure for the superior officer to pay a visit to the office of his subordinate officer and to inquire about the current situation. It would be normal for the two of them to have a tete-a-tete, as you have put it. I believe that this was normal, and I believe that my commander General Hadzihasanovic indeed did that. I'm sure that he did have an informal meeting in the 3rd Corps command prior to the beginning of the meeting. I fully believe that. I believe that they did have a tete-a-tete meeting, the two of them must have met, my commander and Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move on now to a meeting which took place in May. You provided some information to the Trial Chamber in respect of this meeting. Can you confirm that you said that General Halilovic at that point appointed both Delic and Mahmuljin to contact the mujahedin; and if so, what were they supposed to do about the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm having another problem with the interpretation. According to the interpreters, these two were appointed to deal with the problem of the mujahedin. This is not what I said, Your Honours. I said that they were tasked with addressing the problem of mujahedin. I never saw a written order ordering them to be appointed to deal with the problem of mujahedin. I believe that Mr. Delic and Mr. Mahmuljin were not ordered to do that. It was just said that these two members of the supreme command were to address the issue of the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, what in your opinion was the tasking? What were they supposed to do with respect to the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can tell you what they were supposed to do and what they did. They were members of the superior command, and it was not my place as a subordinate officer to ask them what my superior command was up to. At least in the situation when the general principles of security and the main mission of the 3rd Corps were not jeopardised. The main mission was not jeopardised. If it had been, then I would have asked them why they were doing what they were doing. As things were what they were, I did not have the right to ask my superior officers what they were doing and what they intended to do with regard to the issue of the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your opinion, General, was there one group of mujahedin, or were there many groups of mujahedin to deal with for Mr. Delic and Mr. Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified about that. I said that according to our information, this was a very mobile group, a small group of mujahedin who were very mobile. We were not able to determine their number. I've already testified about that. We could not even establish their exact location. I've already -- I've also testified that the security services took measures, I suppose they followed them. They recorded their moves. However, it was very difficult to be sure about how many groups there were. If we had known how many groups there were, we would have also known how many troops there were. We didn't know how many men were there among them. I didn't have that information. I don't know whether the members of the supreme command could determine at the time whether there was one group or two groups consisting of 20, 30 or more men. I know that when I came across one group, there were about 10 to 15 men in that group as far as I could see at that moment. Your Honours, I really can't give you any more precise answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One of the next issues that was discussed with the Trial Chamber was the letter which was sent by General Hadzihasanovic to the supreme command. And in response to a question, you said that you could not say for sure why General Hadzihasanovic decided to send this letter at this specific time. Now, in your opinion, could there be a link between the sending of the letter on 13 June and your encounter with mujahedin who wanted to blow up the monastery in the days preceding the sending of the letter?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to establish a link between these two events. Truth be told, both events are rather interesting. However, it is very difficult for me to establish any sort of link between the two of them. I know, however, that the activities carried out by the supreme command staff from the moment when they received their task, which was in May, until the moment when the letter was written in June did not yield major results with respect to the mujahedin. I suppose that the corps commander was not happy and that he himself wanted to address a letter to the supreme command staff asking them to speed up their solution to the problem of mujahedin, which was growing by the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you knew at that time that General Delic was now the commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like to know if in your opinion you were under the impression that Mahmuljin still had the tasking to meet with the mujahedin and to try and solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness Exhibit DH165/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, one quick question with this document: The last paragraph, we see that there are some letters in capital letters saying "I am requesting your stances and opinions." Is it normal for a commander of a corps in writing a memo to his superior command to put something in capital letters the way he did, and what does this indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This indicates to me that this was very important. General Enver Hadzihasanovic insisted on receiving stances and positions and views of his superior commander, the commander of the Main Staff of the BiH Army. This is the way I interpret what I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You've already had the chance yesterday to answer many questions with respect to this letter. But can you simply confirm, reading the second paragraph, that there was no way for General Hadzihasanovic to communicate with the mujahedin and that these people had already been invited to join the army following proposals of the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read in this paragraph that they wanted to communicate with the leading people of the Main Staff of the BiH Army, rather than with the commander of the 3rd Corps. In their opinion, he was only supposed to call a meeting with the aforementioned people, not to communicate with them. They only wanted to communicate with the leading personnel of the Main Staff of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned under many forms that there were never any mujahedin under control or within the 3rd Corps in 1993. Is that in essence your testimony before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I have problems with the way things are interpreted to me. Before this Trial Chamber, I have already testified that the problem could be divided into two parts. I cannot say that for the entire 1993, as I have heard it in my own language. We are talking about the period up to the moment when the official order was issued to establish the El Mujahedin detachment which was in August 1993 and thereafter. I claim that up to the moment when the order was issued in the month of August 1993, foreigners had never been on the strength of the BiH Army in any capacity. As from the month of August 1993, these foreigners were formally and legally placed under the command of the 3rd Corps. However, I have given you a lot of example showing to you that they never wanted to obey any of the orders issued to them by the 3rd Corps command. I have spoken at great length about that. And I also said that we had problems with the foreigners all throughout my stay with the 3rd Corps. I really have to be very, very precise here. I don't want to contradict my own testimony. So let's say we have this period leading up to August 1993 and the period after August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P294.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, I have four questions left, and this will be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four questions, four minutes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, can you look at this document, which is dated 10 December 1993, and provide me your opinion as to whether you agree that this document shows that there were still foreign mercenaries completely outside of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the 3rd Corps as of 10 December 1993.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is confirmed by this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, will you agree with me that even though you were shown a document with the word "mujahedin" yesterday which dated back to January, is there any reason to believe that the situation in January of 1993 was different than what it was in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said something about that. The situation was somewhat different during that period of time. However, the service which dealt with these issues had information that there were some mercenaries there, and they wanted information. They wanted intelligence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you split up the year 1993 into two, and I have one question for each part. Until the creation of the El Mujahedin unit, would it have been possible for you to stop the mujahedin, to order them not to do some activities, or to punish them for doing so without having to fight them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, in the second part of 1993, after the creation on paper of the El Mujahid, and even though some orders were issued to them, was it possible for you to stop them from taking part in certain activities or to punish them for doing so without having to fight them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the specific situation. One would have to assess the situation. At the moment a breach of discipline takes place and the corps command learns of that or there is a suspicion that a crime was committed by a member of the El Mujahedin detachment, he would be treated the same as any other member of the 3rd Corps. Thus, it depended on the situation, on the specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I just have one last question. And that's more of a gift for you. I would just like to read you a question, because this relates to a document which has been used by the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are already running late. But we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in open session, I would like to say that your testimony is now finished. You have answered the questions of both parties for two weeks. We would like to thank you for your contribution in this search for truth. We wish you a happy journey back home, and I wish you a pleasant retirement. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for having allowed me to testify before this Honourable Court which I deem to be the most Honourable Court in the world. I'm always willing to respond to the invitation by this Chamber to testify. Thank you once again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have worked for five additional minutes. I apologise to the interpreters. This is the last hearing this year. We'll be resuming on the 10th of January at 2.15. I wish you and all your families all the best for the new year and have a good rest before we resume in January. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
